title: Bitwise Operators and Number Representation
summary: AND, OR, XOR, NOT, and the shifts are the five primitives every bit-manipulation trick is built from. Learn how they act bit-by-bit, how two's complement makes negative numbers behave, and the traps that catch candidates in interviews.

slides.markdown:
Every value a computer touches is, underneath, a row of bits. **Bitwise operators** let you read and rewrite those rows directly — no arithmetic, no branching, just AND, OR, XOR, NOT, and the two shifts.

This group builds entirely on five primitives you'll meet in this topic: the four boolean operators applied bit-by-bit, and left/right shift. Everything later — masks, XOR tricks, popcount, subset enumeration — is these five primitives composed in different orders.

Get comfortable here first. Almost every bug in this group traces back to a misunderstanding of how one of these five behaves on a signed integer.

slides.subTitle: AND, OR, XOR, NOT, and the shifts
slides.markdown:
Each operator acts **independently on every bit position** — there's no carrying between positions, which is what makes them fast and predictable.

| Operator | Per-bit rule | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `&` AND | 1 only if both bits are 1 | test or clear bits |
| `\|` OR | 1 if either bit is 1 | set bits |
| `^` XOR | 1 if bits differ | toggle bits, find differences |
| `~` NOT | flips every bit | build masks, invert |
| `<<` `>>` shift | slides bits left/right | scale by powers of two |

No position ever looks at its neighbor. `5 & 3` is decided one bit column at a time, which is exactly why these run in a single CPU cycle regardless of how large the number is.

slides.subTitle: Side by side
slides.markdown:
Take one byte, `a = 1011 0010`, against a second byte `b = 0110 1100`, and watch how each operator reshapes it.

`a & b` keeps only the columns where both have a 1. `a | b` keeps a column wherever either has a 1. `a ^ b` keeps a column only where they disagree. `~a` flips every single column of `a` alone, with no second operand.

Seeing all four side by side on the same bytes makes the difference concrete rather than abstract: AND and OR both need two matching 1s or at least one 1 respectively; XOR is the "exactly one" operator; NOT is unary and touches every bit unconditionally.

slides.subTitle: Why negative numbers behave the way they do
slides.markdown:
Signed integers are stored in **two's complement**: to negate a number, flip every bit and add 1. `5` is `0000 0101`; flip to `1111 1010`, add 1, get `1111 1011` — that's `-5`.

This representation is chosen because it makes addition **just work** without special-casing sign. `5 + (-5)` in two's complement is `0000 0101 + 1111 1011 = 1 0000 0000`, and dropping the overflowed top bit leaves exactly `0`.

One consequence worth memorizing: the top bit is the sign bit, so an n-bit signed type ranges from `-2^(n-1)` to `2^(n-1) - 1` — one more negative value than positive, because `0` only needs one pattern.

slides.subTitle: And where that stops being true
slides.markdown:
`x << k` is `x * 2^k`, and `x >> k` is `x / 2^k` (floored) — for **non-negative** `x` that fits in the type. Shifting is how hardware multiplies and divides by powers of two in a single cycle instead of running a full multiplier circuit.

It stops being true in two places: **overflow** — `x << k` can shift 1-bits straight off the top, silently discarding them, so `x << k` is not `x * 2^k` once the product exceeds the type's range — and **negative numbers**, where right shift's rounding direction depends on which right shift you use (next slide).

Treat the multiply/divide equivalence as an interview-explaining shortcut, not a guarantee you can lean on in production code without checking the type width first.

`>>` on a negative number can mean two different things, and which one you get depends on the language:

- **Arithmetic shift** (`>>` in Java, C, C++, Python) copies the **sign bit** into the newly-opened positions. `-8 >> 1` stays negative: `-4`. This preserves the sign, which is what you want for ordinary division-like behavior.
- **Logical shift** (`>>>` in Java, `>>>` in JavaScript) always fills with **0**, ignoring sign. Applied to the same bit pattern, `-8 >>> 1` produces a huge positive number, because the bit pattern for `-8` is reinterpreted as unsigned.

Mixing these up is a classic interview bug: reaching for `>>` to divide a negative number and getting a correctly-negative-but-wrong-magnitude result, or reaching for `>>>` on a value you actually wanted to keep signed.

`x << 32` on a 32-bit `int` looks like it should produce `0` — every bit shifted out, nothing left. In several languages it does **not** behave that way at all.

In C and C++, shifting by an amount greater than or equal to the type's bit width is **undefined behavior** — the compiler is free to do anything, including something that looks like it works today and breaks under a different optimization level. In Java, the shift amount is silently taken **modulo the bit width**, so `x << 32` on an `int` is actually `x << 0`, i.e. `x` unchanged — a very common source of "why didn't this become zero" bugs.

Always guard shift amounts against the type's width explicitly; never assume a shift "saturates" to zero.

In C, C++, Java, and several other languages, bitwise operators bind **looser** than comparison operators — the opposite of what most people guess.

So `if (x & 1 == 0)` does not check "is `x` even." It parses as `x & (1 == 0)`, which evaluates the comparison first, producing a boolean `0` or `1`, and ANDs `x` against *that*. The condition silently tests the wrong thing and rarely crashes, it just gives wrong answers.

The fix is mechanical: **always parenthesize a bitwise expression before comparing it** — `if ((x & 1) == 0)`. Python sidesteps this particular trap (its bitwise operators also bind looser than comparisons, but chained comparisons make the failure mode different), but the parenthesize-defensively habit is worth keeping everywhere.

slides.subTitle: Across common interview languages
slides.markdown:
What happens when a bitwise or arithmetic result overflows the type's range differs by language and by signedness:

| Language / type | Signed overflow | Unsigned overflow |
|---|---|---|
| C / C++ `int` | undefined behavior | wraps modulo 2^n, well-defined |
| Java `int`/`long` | wraps silently (always two's complement) | no unsigned integer type exists |
| Python `int` | never overflows — arbitrary precision | n/a |
| JavaScript (`\|0`, `>>>0`) | bitwise ops coerce to 32-bit, then wrap | `>>>` yields unsigned 32-bit wrap |

The practical takeaway: in C/C++ a signed overflow is a bug waiting to happen (compilers may assume it never occurs and optimize accordingly), while Java and JavaScript guarantee a wraparound you can reason about, and Python simply grows the integer instead of overflowing at all.

Bitwise operators are attractive for more than cleverness — they're **one CPU cycle each**, with no branching and no memory allocation, which is why they show up wherever performance matters.

Concrete places this shows up: **bloom filters** hash a key into a handful of bit positions and OR them into a bitset — checking membership is a few ANDs. **Flags and permission bits** (file mode `rwxrwxrwx`, a feature-flag register) pack dozens of booleans into one integer instead of dozens of separate fields. **Hash functions** (FNV, xxHash) lean on XOR and shift because they're branch-free and pipeline cleanly.

The pattern to notice: whenever a problem's state is "a small fixed set of yes/no facts," a bitwise-encoded integer is usually faster and smaller than an array of booleans.

slides.sectionTitle: What the rest of this group builds
slides.markdown:
Everything ahead composes these five primitives: `bit-idioms` turns AND/OR/XOR/shift into the get/set/clear/toggle recipe every masking question uses; `xor-tricks` exploits XOR's self-canceling property; `bit-counting` builds fast popcount out of AND with a shifted self; and `bitmask-subsets` uses a whole integer as a compact representation of a set.

If you can predict, without running code, what `x & (x - 1)` or `x << 3` does to a specific bit pattern — including on a negative `x` — you have everything you need for the rest of this group.
